title: LinkedIn Recruiter InMail credit limits: monthly credits, daily caps and fixes for Mac
metaTitle: LinkedIn Recruiter InMail credit limits: Mac guide
description: Recruiter seats get 150 InMail credits a month and a 1,000 daily cap. Learn how credits refund, what the 13% response rule means, and how to stay under both.
secondaryKeywords: linkedin recruiter inmail limit per day
problem: inmail credit and daily send limits
intro: LinkedIn Recruiter gives each seat 150 InMail credits a month, a daily cap of 1,000 InMails and a 13% response rate floor. Run out of credits and you wait for renewal. Let the response rate slip and LinkedIn can pause bulk InMail for two weeks. This page covers each limit, the numbers behind it, and fixes you can use today without buying anything.
tldr: Recruiter seats get 150 InMail credits a month. Open Profile InMails are a separate allowance and do not use those credits.
A seat can send up to 1,000 InMails a day. The bigger risk for most recruiters is the 13% response rate rule on 100 or more InMails per 14 days.
Credits come back when a candidate accepts, declines, or replies within 90 days. A message with no answer keeps its credit spent.
LinkedIn's talent blog reports that InMails under 400 characters get replies about 22% above average. Use short, personal messages.
Track credits and response rate in a sheet every week, so a warning never surprises you.

blocks.text: You can hit the InMail wall in three ways. The monthly credit pool can run dry before renewal. A new seat can get blocked in its first week. Or your response rate can fall under 13%, and bulk sending gets paused. Each one needs a different fix, so start by finding out which limit you are near.
How many monthly InMail credits LinkedIn Recruiter gives you

LinkedIn's help page for Recruiter and Recruiter Lite lists 150 monthly InMail credits for Recruiter. Recruiter Lite gets 30. RPS gets 100. The same page says extra packs can be purchased for Recruiter. These allowances are per seat, so a team with five seats has five separate pools, not one shared stack.

rows: Extra credit packs can be purchased
Renewal page lists a maximum balance of 120
Listed on the Recruiter help page
Does not count toward monthly credits
blocks.caption: Monthly allowances from LinkedIn Help. Confirm on the live page.

blocks.text: Open Profile InMails are the part people miss. The same help page says Recruiter and RPS seats get 350 Open Profile InMails per seat each calendar month. Those do not use monthly credits. The Recruiter Lite figure on that page disagrees with itself, so check the live table before you plan around it.

Premium InMail credits are a different pool. LinkedIn's credit page says Premium InMail credits cannot be used on Sales Navigator or Recruiter. Credits do not transfer when you upgrade. A canceled Premium subscription resets the balance to zero. If your team mixes Premium and Recruiter accounts, do not count one pool as the other.
The daily InMail cap and the new seat first-week limit

The daily limit is 1,000 InMails per seat per day. Going over it triggers a notification. That cap is high. For most individual recruiters, the monthly credits and the response rate run out first. New seats work differently. LinkedIn's help page says a new seat has a first-week cap of 200 InMails.

blocks.title: New seat in week one
blocks.text: A new seat that sends more than 200 InMails in its first week loses the service until that week ends. Plan the first week for 200 or fewer. Use the days before your first send to build your list and tighten your message.
How InMail credits come back after a reply

LinkedIn returns an InMail credit when the recipient accepts, declines, or replies within 90 days of sending. Pending messages do not trigger a refund. Quick Replies count as a response. A message that gets no answer within 90 days keeps its credit spent, so silence has a real cost.

The response definitions differ across LinkedIn pages. The Recruiter policy counts an InMail reply, an accepted invitation, or a Not Interested reply. The Recruiter InMail Report counts accepted plus declined, divided by total sent, using only responses within 30 days. Your dashboard and your refund window will not always match, so track both.
The 13% response rate rule for Recruiter InMail

The response rate rule surprises people most. LinkedIn's Recruiter InMail Policy sets a 13% threshold. A rate below 13% over a 14-day period triggers a warning. Repeated breaches can lead to an InMail Improvement Period. A separate LinkedIn page says the threshold applies to 100 or more InMails in each 14-day assessment period.

During an Improvement Period, bulk InMail is disabled for 2 weeks. You get out by sending one-to-one messages that lift the rate above 13%. If you do not, the restriction continues for another 14 days. The policy pages describe the warning timing differently, so read the live policy before you plan around exact dates.

Here is the simple version. Say you send 100 InMails in a 14-day period. To stay at the line, you need at least 13 responses. Twelve replies on 100 messages falls under 13%, however good the messages look. The rule measures reply rate, not how many messages you sent.
Message length, timing and targeting that lift replies

LinkedIn's Talent Blog looked at tens of millions of corporate recruiter InMails sent from May 2021 to April 2022. The analysis is observational and self-reported. Read the numbers as patterns, not guarantees, but they are the best public signal available for message design.

items: Under 400 characters: response rate about 22% above average.
Over 1,200 characters: response rate about 11% below average.
Individually sent InMails: response rates roughly 15% higher than bulk InMails.
Friday about 4% below average, Saturday about 8% below, Sunday to Thursday within about 1% of average.
65% of responses arrive within 24 hours, and 90% arrive within one week.

blocks.text: Targeting matters too. The same analysis says candidates in Recommended Matches are up to 35% more likely to accept an InMail than candidates found through search alone. Open to Work candidates have a response rate about 37% higher. Spend credits on those people first, and holding the 13% line gets easier.
Watch the timing. Send on Sunday to Thursday when you can. The Friday and Saturday drop is small, but it is a drop. Your credits are fixed for the month, so every weak send uses up part of the pool.
What a seat transfer means for the response rate

LinkedIn's Recruiter InMail Policy says that when a seat is transferred, the new seat holder is accountable for the previous recruiter's response rate. If you inherit a seat, open its InMail Report before your first send. Find out whether the seat already sits near the 13% line. A clean start beats a surprise warning in week two.
Are recruiters under more pressure than before?

The Employ 2026 Recruiter Nation report, fielded by Zogby among more than 1,200 US HR recruiters and managers, says 36% find recruiting more stressful than a year earlier. That is down from 45% in 2025 and 54% in 2024. The top stressor is AI-polished resumes, named by 33%. Employ sells recruiting software, so treat the trend as a signal, not a verdict.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics counts 939,700 human resources specialists in 2025, including recruitment specialists. It projects 6% growth from 2025 to 2035. BLS describes recruitment specialists as people who find, screen, and interview applicants. The field is large, so small habits around limits add up across a team.
A weekly routine that keeps you under the InMail limits

items: Monday: open the InMail Report. Write down credits left, the 14-day response rate and the renewal date.
Tuesday to Thursday: send one-to-one messages under 400 characters to candidates you filtered for fit.
Thursday afternoon: mark accepted, declined and replied outcomes in your tracker, so the rate stays current.
Friday: keep sends light, since Friday responses run below average in LinkedIn's data.
Any day your rate nears 13%: send one-to-one messages only until it recovers.

blocks.text: Track InMail credits and response rate in Google Sheets

A simple tracker beats memory. Make one row per InMail. Use columns for date, candidate, type, and outcome. Put InMail or Open Profile in column C. Put Accepted, Declined, Replied, or blank in column D. Keep the sheet open in Chrome next to Recruiter. The [recruiter tracker setup guide](/for/recruiters/google-sheets) shows a layout you can copy.

Count today's sends with a formula in an empty cell: =COUNTIFS(A:A, TODAY(), C:C, "InMail"). For the whole month, use =COUNTIFS(A:A, ">="&DATE(2026,11,1), C:C, "InMail") and change the date for other months. When you paste candidate names from a LinkedIn page, use ⌘⇧V to paste plain values only. Edit > Paste special > Values only does the same thing from the menu.

For the response rate, count Accepted and Declined over all InMails sent: =(COUNTIFS(D:D, "Accepted")+COUNTIFS(D:D, "Declined"))/COUNTIFS(C:C, "InMail"). Then select the cell and set Format > Number > Percent. Treat the result as your estimate. LinkedIn's policy also counts replies, so check the official report before you act on a warning.
Mistakes that burn InMail credits fastest

items: Sending one template to a whole search result. Individually sent messages get replies about 15% higher than bulk in LinkedIn's data.
Writing more than 1,200 characters of company history before the role. Long messages land about 11% below average.
Forgetting that pending messages do not refund. A quiet candidate keeps the credit spent.
Assuming your sheet matches the dashboard. The windows and definitions differ between LinkedIn pages.
Inheriting a seat without checking its response rate first. The new holder carries the old rate.
Mixing Premium and Recruiter credits. They are separate pools and do not transfer on upgrade.

blocks.text: Where Lazur helps with LinkedIn InMail limits, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. Hold ⌥⌘, ask about what is on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. It can point at the credit counter, explain a warning banner, draft a short message for you to edit, and dictate notes with fn. It does not send InMails, change your seat, or buy packs.

Lazur only knows what appears on your screen and what you say. It cannot confirm a LinkedIn policy by itself. Ask it to research the live help pages. Its research runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs and comes back with a summary, and you should open the pages yourself to check the wording.

Explain what the 13% rule means for the seat you hold right now.
Draft a short, personal InMail for you to edit and send yourself.
Dictate a candidate note into your tracker with fn.
Not a fit: sending messages, changing seat settings, or buying credits for you.

blocks.title: Candidate data comes first
blocks.text: Candidate details can be personal data. Follow your employer's rules on what you may paste into an AI tool. Keep names and contact details out of drafts unless your policy allows them.
What to do this week

Open the InMail Report today. Write down your credits left, your 14-day response rate, and the date your month renews. Pick one fix from this page and try it for two weeks. Compare your rate after 14 days, not after one good day. For questions about more seats or packs, check LinkedIn's pricing or talk to your LinkedIn account contact.

faq.question: Do LinkedIn InMail credits roll over for Recruiter?
faq.answer: LinkedIn's credit page describes monthly renewal but does not list rollover for full Recruiter. Third-party guides give different rollover caps, so treat carryover as unresolved. Check the live Recruiter help page or ask your LinkedIn account contact before you plan on it.

faq.question: Does an Open Profile InMail use a monthly credit?
faq.answer: No. LinkedIn's help page says Open Profile InMails do not count toward monthly InMail credits. The same page lists 350 per seat per calendar month for Recruiter and RPS. Confirm the figure on the live page for your plan.

faq.question: What counts as a response for the 13% rule?
faq.answer: LinkedIn's Recruiter InMail Policy counts an InMail reply, an accepted invitation, or a Not Interested reply. The InMail Report counts accepted plus declined, divided by total sent, within 30 days. The definitions differ, so check the report before you act on a warning.

faq.question: How long do I have to get a credit back?
faq.answer: Credits come back when a candidate accepts, declines, or replies within 90 days of sending. A pending message does not trigger a refund. Quick Replies count as a response, according to LinkedIn's credit page.

faq.question: Can Lazur send InMails or change my seat for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons or operate LinkedIn for you. It points at things on your screen, explains warnings, drafts text and dictates notes. You send every message yourself.

faq.question: Is the weekly connection invite limit about 100?
faq.answer: Some third-party blogs say about 100 connection invites a week. This research found no official LinkedIn source for that figure, so do not plan around it. Use LinkedIn's own message if you hit a limit.

faq.question: Does Lazur store what I say or what is on my screen?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. Your content is never used to train AI models.

faq.question: What changes if I recruit for regulated roles like nursing or accounting?
faq.answer: The LinkedIn limits stay the same. Candidate records for regulated roles can carry extra rules. Follow your employer's rules on client or patient data before you paste anything into Lazur or a sheet.

costs.title: Credits spent on silence
costs.text: Every InMail with no answer within 90 days keeps its credit spent. Pending messages do not refund. A batch of quiet messages can use up the monthly pool before renewal. Track replies every week, so you spot a quiet batch early and stop feeding it credits.

costs.title: Bulk outreach paused
costs.text: Below 13% over a 14-day period triggers a warning. A repeat can lead to an Improvement Period, where bulk InMail is disabled for 2 weeks. You exit by sending one-to-one messages that lift the rate. Otherwise the restriction runs another 14 days.

costs.title: A blocked first week on a new seat
costs.text: A new seat that sends more than 200 InMails in its first week loses the service until the week ends. A recruiter who starts a new seat during a busy sourcing week can lose days of outreach. Plan the first week in advance.

costs.title: Stress you carry from week to week
costs.text: The Employ 2026 survey says 36% of recruiters find the job more stressful than a year ago, down from 54% in 2024. Employ sells recruiting software, so treat the figure as a signal. Limits you can see on screen still take some guesswork out of a busy week.

costs.title: Money spent on extra packs
costs.text: LinkedIn's help page says extra Recruiter credit packs can be purchased. The research did not find pack prices on LinkedIn's own pages. Check LinkedIn's pricing before you assume the cost. Do not buy packs to cover a problem that better messages would solve.

causes.title: The credit pool is monthly and fixed
causes.text: Recruiter seats get 150 monthly credits, and Recruiter Lite gets 30. The pool resets on renewal, not when you need it most. Credits do not transfer on upgrade, and a canceled Premium subscription resets its balance to zero. That is why timing and targeting matter more than sending speed.

causes.title: The response rate is checked in 14-day blocks
causes.text: LinkedIn measures response rate within each 14-day assessment period. A quiet batch can drag the rate under 13% even when your next batch is strong. The rule looks at recent sends, so one weak fortnight can matter more than a good month.

causes.title: Bulk and generic messages get fewer replies
causes.text: LinkedIn's talent blog data says individually sent InMails see response rates roughly 15% higher than bulk. A template sent to a long list reads like one, and candidates reply less. Bulk sending also puts the 13% rule at risk faster than personal sends do.

causes.title: Long messages lose attention
causes.text: Under 400 characters beats average by about 22%. Over 1,200 characters sits about 11% below average. In practice, long messages bury the reason for reaching out, and candidates stop reading before they get to it. Shorter messages make the reason obvious in the first two lines.

causes.title: Weekend and Friday sends
causes.text: Friday responses run about 4% below average, and Saturday about 8% below. Sunday to Thursday sits within about 1% of average. The gap is small on any one send, but it compounds when your credits are fixed for the month.

causes.title: Seat transfers carry the old history
causes.text: When a seat transfers, the new seat holder becomes accountable for the previous recruiter's response rate under LinkedIn's policy. You can start a month already close to the 13% line without making a single send.

causes.title: Different windows and definitions
causes.text: LinkedIn uses 30 days in the InMail Report, 90 days for credit refunds, and a separate list of response types in the policy. A number that looks fine on your sheet can differ from the dashboard. Mismatched definitions cause more confusion than any single limit.

fixes.title: Check credits and rate every Monday
fixes.text: Open the InMail Report every Monday. Write credits left, the 14-day response rate, and the renewal date in your tracker. Set a personal warning a few points above 13%, which is your own choice rather than a LinkedIn rule. Act before the line, not after the warning arrives.

fixes.title: Send shorter, personal messages
fixes.text: Keep each InMail under 400 characters. Open with the role and one specific reason the candidate fits. Ask one clear question at the end. LinkedIn's talent blog ties messages under 400 characters to response rates about 22% above average. Test two versions for a week and track which gets replies.

fixes.title: Switch to one-to-one when the rate dips
fixes.text: If your 14-day rate nears 13%, stop bulk sends. LinkedIn says you leave an Improvement Period by sending one-to-one messages that lift the rate above 13%. Start with the candidates who match most closely. Each reply helps the number recover.

fixes.title: Aim credits at Open to Work and Recommended Matches
fixes.text: The talent blog says Open to Work candidates have a response rate about 37% higher. Candidates in Recommended Matches are up to 35% more likely to accept. Filter for those signals before you spend a credit. A smaller, better list can beat a large, weak one.

fixes.title: Send your strongest messages Sunday to Thursday
fixes.text: Send your best messages from Sunday through Thursday. Friday responses run about 4% below average, and Saturday about 8% below. Save your least certain or longest messages for the lighter days, rather than your strongest ones.

fixes.title: Use Open Profile InMails where the candidate qualifies
fixes.text: Open Profile InMails are a separate allowance. LinkedIn lists 350 per seat per calendar month for Recruiter and RPS, and they do not count toward monthly credits. Check eligibility on the live page, then use this allowance for open profiles before you spend credits.

fixes.title: Log every reply the day it arrives
fixes.text: Credits come back when a candidate accepts, declines, or replies within 90 days. Mark each outcome in your sheet the same day. LinkedIn refunds the credit either way, but your log shows which messages work. Without the log, you cannot tell which change helped.

fixes.title: Plan a new or inherited seat before the first send
fixes.text: For a new seat, plan the first week for 200 InMails or fewer. For an inherited seat, read its InMail Report before you send anything. The policy makes the new holder accountable for the previous recruiter's response rate, so the history is yours from day one.

fixes.title: Confirm limits on the live pages and note the date
fixes.text: Several LinkedIn pages disagree. The Recruiter Lite Open Profile figure conflicts inside one page, and the 13% warning wording differs across two policy pages. Treat the live pages as the source of truth. Write down the date you checked, so you know when to check again.

plan.label: Monday
plan.title: Read your numbers
plan.text: Open the InMail Report. Write credits left, the 14-day response rate and the renewal date in your Google Sheet. If you cannot find the counter, ask Lazur to point at it.

plan.label: Tuesday
plan.title: Build a filtered list
plan.text: Filter for Open to Work or Recommended Matches candidates. Draft each InMail under 400 characters, and make every message specific to the candidate's work.

plan.label: Wednesday
plan.title: Send one-to-one
plan.text: Send messages individually, not as a bulk batch. Log each send in column C with the date. If the seat is new, stay under 200 InMails for the week.

plan.label: Thursday
plan.title: Log replies
plan.text: Mark accepted, declined and replied outcomes the same day. Compare your sheet's rate with the InMail Report for the same window, and note any gap.

plan.label: Friday
plan.title: Keep sends light
plan.text: Send fewer InMails on Friday, since responses run below average on that day in LinkedIn's data. Use the time to follow up with accepted candidates in Gmail.

plan.label: Weekly review
plan.title: Decide the next week
plan.text: If the rate is near 13%, send one-to-one messages only. If credits look tight, use Open Profile InMails where eligible. Write the decision in your sheet so next week starts clear.
